segments.say: So far in this video, most of our examples have been about events: a death, an illness, an accident. But some of the most painful shattered assumptions are about people. A friend who lied. A partner who left. A leader, a church, a company or a doctor who was trusted, and who failed. When the thing that breaks is trust, recovery has its own shape, and it's worth looking at on its own.

show.title: When the belief that breaks is about people

segments.say: Jennifer Freyd, a psychologist at the University of Oregon, proposed that betrayal by someone we depend on is a particular kind of harm. Her theory, called betrayal trauma theory, starts from a simple observation. Human beings, especially children, depend on others for survival. When the person who hurts us is also the person we rely on, our minds face an awful dilemma, and sometimes find unusual ways to cope with it.

Freyd argued that harm done by someone close, on whom the victim depends, is different in kind from harm done by a stranger. Because the dependence cannot simply be cut, she suggested, people may limit their awareness of the betrayal in order to continue the relationship that they need. Her theory has been debated and tested over the years, and it's best seen as one influential framework for understanding why betrayal by trusted people can be especially hard to process.

show.what: Betrayal trauma: the logic of forgetting childhood abuse

segments.say: The last item is the heaviest. After being deceived, many people stop trusting not only the other person but also themselves. How did I not see it? Rebuilding trust, then, includes rebuilding trust in your own judgment, and that takes time, and a different kind of evidence than the first time around.

show.title: Why betrayal hits differently
items: We depend on the person who hurt us
It breaks our ability to judge who is safe
It attacks the belief that people are mostly good
It can make us doubt our own judgment

segments.say: Betrayal doesn't only come from individuals. It can come from organisations, such as a school, a hospital, a military unit, a church or an employer, that we trusted to protect us. Researchers have given this a name of its own, and have found that it adds to the harm.

Carly Smith and Jennifer Freyd described institutional betrayal as wrongdoing by an institution upon individuals who depend on it, including failures to prevent harm, and failures to respond supportively afterwards. They proposed that such betrayal can increase the distress of the people affected, on top of the original harm. In their later studies, students who reported institutional betrayal related to their experiences tended to report more distress than those who did not.

This helps to explain something that many people find confusing. They are hurt by an event, and then hurt again by how those in charge responded. A denial, a cover-up or a cold shoulder can wound as deeply as the original harm. If this has happened to you, the second injury is real, and it is not oversensitivity.

A related idea comes from the study of war. Soldiers and other people in high-stakes jobs sometimes carry a particular kind of wound. It doesn't come from fear alone. It comes from doing, seeing or failing to prevent something that violates their deepest sense of right and wrong. Researchers call this moral injury.

Brett Litz and his colleagues described moral injury as the lasting emotional, psychological and spiritual harm that can follow a morally troubling event, whether caused by oneself or by others. They proposed that it's linked to feelings of guilt, shame and a shattered sense of trust, and that helping people recover may involve rebuilding a sense of moral worth and connection, as well as treating fear-based symptoms.

show.who: Litz, Stein, Delaney, Lebowitz, Nash, Silva & Maguen
show.what: Moral injury and moral repair in war veterans: a preliminary model and intervention strategy

segments.say: The concept began with war, but it has since been applied to health care workers, journalists, police officers and others. What it shares with our topic is the shattered assumption at its heart: the belief that the world, or I, am fundamentally good. When that breaks, people need more than rest. They need a way to restore their moral footing.

show.title: Moral injury and ordinary life
items: Nurses forced to ration care
Employees told to ignore harm
Soldiers who acted against their values
Anyone who sees something deeply wrong and cannot stop it

segments.say: How can trust be rebuilt, once it's broken? Research on relationships and on repair suggests a few ingredients. They won't guarantee a result, and in some cases the right answer is to leave. But they describe what real repair looks like when it's possible.

Notice that every item on the list is about time and consistency. Trust is rebuilt not by promises but by a track record. And it's rebuilt in small steps: a promise kept, then another, then another, until the evidence outweighs the memory of the betrayal. If the other person isn't willing to do these things, you're allowed to stop trying.

show.title: What repair tends to need
items: An honest account of what happened
A genuine apology without excuses
Changed behaviour over time
Patience from both sides

segments.say: You don't have to choose between trusting everyone and trusting no one. After a betrayal, many people find a middle path: they trust in small amounts, in specific areas, and adjust as evidence comes in. That isn't naive and it isn't cynical. It's how a thoughtful person rebuilds a worldview after a break, with open eyes.

Four terms from this chapter. Betrayal trauma is harm done by someone we depend on. Institutional betrayal is harm by, or a failed response from, an organisation we rely on. Moral injury is the lasting wound of violating, or witnessing a violation of, our deepest values. And repair is the process of restoring trust. Picture this scene. A woman discovers that her business partner has been quietly taking money for years. Beyond the loss, what hurts most is that she cannot trust her own memory of the friendship. Was any of it real? Her counsellor does not tell her. Instead, she asks what she knew then, and what she knows now, and suggests that her judgment was reasonable given what she had been shown. Slowly, the woman begins to trust her own mind again, and then, in small steps, to trust other people. Repair began with the account of what happened, and not with forgiveness.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Betrayal trauma
Institutional betrayal
Moral injury
Repair

segments.say: Here are some gentle steps, drawing on what we have discussed. First, notice that your reaction is normal. Distrust after a betrayal is not a flaw, it is information. Second, decide what you are ready to trust again, and what you're not yet ready to. You can trust a colleague with a task before you trust them with a secret. Third, give trust in small steps, and watch what happens. Let people earn the next step. And fourth, talk to someone safe about how it has affected you. Betrayal makes people lonely, and the loneliness is part of the injury, so the remedy includes company. If the betrayal involved abuse or serious harm, a trained counsellor can help, and that's not a sign of weakness. It is exactly the kind of problem such people are trained to help with.

show.title: If your trust has been broken
items: Notice that your reaction is normal
Decide what you are ready to trust again, and what not yet
Give trust in small steps and watch what happens
Talk to someone safe about how it has affected you

segments.say: A bowl, broken and mended with gold. It's a picture borrowed from the Japanese art of kintsugi, and it's often used as a symbol of repair. It's worth remembering that the mended bowl isn't the same as the original. It's a different object, with a history, and for many people that's the only honest kind of repair there is.

If you have been betrayed, and you now find yourself careful, you haven't become cold. You've learned something expensive. Caution can sit alongside warmth, and the best relationships after a betrayal are often the ones in which both people understand why the care is needed.

So what did we learn? That betrayal by someone we depend on hurts in its own way. That institutions can add a second injury. That moral injury is a wound to our sense of right. And that trust is rebuilt slowly, in small steps, and sometimes only partly.
In the next chapter, we'll turn to the people on the outside. When someone we love is hurting, what helps and what does harm, and why so many well-meant sentences miss.
